newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan plans eurobond in 97, seeks ratings rise.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan plans eurobond in 97, seeks ratings rise.

text.p: Oil-rich Kazakstan is considering either a Samurai or eurobond for issue this year after the government has made efforts to improve the country's credit rating for sovereign debt, a senior Kazakh minister said.

"We hope Kazakhstan's credit rating will be improved," Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Pavlov told a news conference. A better credit rating was needed for new borrowings on international markets, he said.
Pavlov said the government was considering various types of Eurobond or Samurai bonds to help reduce debts to pensioners.
Last November, international rating agencies Moody's and Standard and Poor's gave the former Soviet republic Ba3 and BB- ratings respectively for long-term foreign currency debt.
In December, Kazakhstan placed its debut Eurobond on international markets. The $200 million issue, double the planned amount, was snapped up by investors.
Dutch bank ABN AMRO Hoare Govett organised the bond for the Central Asian republic, which was priced to yield 9.3 percent, or 3.5 percentage points above comparable U.S. Treasury notes.
Pavlov said loans were needed to promote pension reform.

"The reform will start in 1998, but already this year we will face a problem -- what to do with the debts amassed by the (state) pension fund," Pavlov said. He added that unpaid pensions totalled 34 billion tenge ($450 million).
Asked when the issues would be placed on international markets, the minister said: "Most probably, this year", but gave no further details.
Nor did he say how the government was planning to improve the country's credit rating.
Experts point at Kazakhstan's tight credit and monetary policies, a realistic 1997 state budget and the stable tenge currency as factors which could boost the rating.
